/WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Issued at 320 AM MST Mon Nov 23 2026

Winds will gradually decrease Wednesday as the split trough moves 
away from the area. Our slow warming trend will continue, with areas 
along and west of I-25 jumping perhaps 3-5F from Tuesday, while the 
Nebraska panhandle sees similar temperatures. while a very weak vort-
max will pass through the area Wednesday night, the only notable 
impact looks like some more cloud cover overnight. Thanksgiving day 
looks quite pleasant across the area, with decreasing cloud cover 
and temperatures returning to above seasonal averages. Look for 
highs in the low to mid 50s for the High Plains, and 40s around 
Laramie and Rawlins. Winds should be light to breezy for most of the 
day on Thursday, but could be increasing by the end of the day. 

An interesting and challenging forecast is setting up for the Friday 
through Sunday period. As of now, there is medium confidence through 
about Friday, and then confidence completely falls apart for 
Saturday and Sunday with wildly different model solutions possible. 
To start the active period, a very powerful moisture laden Pacific 
jet stream is favored to surge into the Pacific northwest on 
Thanksgiving Day, with the nose of the jet streak encroaching on our 
area by the evening/overnight hours. This will be developing on the 
fringe of a strong, organized ridge building into the southwest
US and associated with a sharp temperature gradient. Initially,
we should be solidly south of the temperature gradient. This 
puts us in the right exit region of the jet streak, where 
synoptic subsidence is favored. As a result, expect winds to 
increase Thursday night for the wind prone areas, spreading into
the Plains on Friday. LREF median 700-mb winds are around 45 to
50 knots, with several members closer to 60 knots. This is a 
pretty good signal for high winds at this lead time, suggesting 
potential for a middle-tier high wind event at least for the 
wind prone areas, possibly spreading into adjacent zones. For 
the typical gap areas, in-house guidance is quite aggressive, 
giving a 70%-80% probability for high winds. More likely than 
not, Friday will be another mild day, but there is a little bit 
of bust potential on forecast highs if the cold front arrives 
earlier than expected. The jet will also have a fair amount of 
deep moisture with it, increasing the chances for orographic 
mountain snowfall beginning Friday. 

Ensemble consensus completely falls apart Saturday onwards with a 
remarkably large spread between extremes. The suite is just about 
evenly split between two highly divergent scenarios. The key piece 
of the puzzle is the strength of the ridge moving into the southwest 
CONUS. In the first scenario, the ridge is quite strong and also 
progresses eastward more rapidly, nudging the jet off to the north 
for the weekend. This would shut off the mountain-snow tap and lead 
to a significant warm-up for much of the area. The jet will still be 
close enough that even in this scenario, the potential for high 
winds will persist through Saturday and Sunday. The mountains 
would still likely see some snow, but amounts would be much 
lower due to the shorter duration of moist orographic ascent. 
Some precipitation spreading into the plains could still be 
possible in this scenario as the ridge lifts to the northeast 
(overrunning ascent) in the Friday night time frame. The other 
scenario involves the upper level ridge coming in slightly 
weaker and slower. The result keeps the jet near or even just 
south of our area Saturday and Sunday, pushing the temperature 
gradient through our area, probably around Friday night. This 
would continue moist orographic ascent in the mountains through 
Saturday and Sunday, and result in dramatically colder 
temperatures for the High Plains. In addition, an arctic front 
stalled somewhere across our area would suggest the possibility 
for frontogenetic and overrunning ascent, and thus higher 
chances for snow to spread into the plains. As far as forecast 
outcome, the first scenario would mean highs Saturday and Sunday
in the 50s to low 60s and largely dry, while the second 
scenario would keep us shivering in the 20s and 30s with snow 
showers possible! NBM guidance is essentially an average of 
these two scenarios, and thus is likely to be wrong, but it's 
impossible to say in which direction. Therefore, it is not 
prudent to differ from NBM guidance significantly with models 
more or less evenly split. This period will need to be closely 
monitored in the coming days.
